subject: Business Models
title: Colonial Plantations
description: A quick win: understand Colonial Plantations.

hook.text: Sugar, tobacco, and cotton plantations were the first global supply chains. Demand was insatiable.

buildup.text: Plantations used forced labor to produce raw materials cheaply for European consumption.

discovery.text: The plantation model was vertically integrated: grow, process, and ship from a single operation.

twist.text: This efficiency came at a monstrous human cost. Profit depended on exploitation, not innovation.

climax.text: Modern supply chains still echo plantation logic: cheap production far away, consumption nearby.

punchline.text: Cheap goods, hidden costs. Supply chains carry history.

quiz.question: What was the key 'advantage' of the plantation model?

details.summary: Colonial plantations were large-scale agricultural operations that used enslaved or coerced labor to mass-produce export crops like sugar, cotton, tobacco, and rubber..
details.whyItMatters: Plantations were the first global supply chains, connecting colonized production to European consumption. Understanding their economics reveals how forced labor subsidized Western development and established agricultural and trade patterns that.
takeaways: Plantations applied factory-level organization to agricultural commodity production
Forced and enslaved labor kept production costs artificially low for maximum profit
Sugar, cotton, and tobacco plantations drove the colonial economy for centuries

faq.question: How were plantations organized as proto-industrial businesses?
faq.answer: Plantations used division of labor, standardized processes, capital-intensive equipment, and accounting systems centuries before factories. Sugar plantations had specialized teams for planting, harvesting, processing, and shipping..

faq.question: What was the economic impact of plantation agriculture?
faq.answer: Plantation profits funded European industrial growth, banking systems, and further colonial expansion. Cotton from American plantations supplied British textile mills. Sugar profits built Caribbean port cities..
